correctness.rationale: The exact \(k\)-th power has fixed points iff \(g\) centralizes \(q=h^k\) and \(g^k(x)=q(x)\). Uniform elements of \(C(q)\) have wreath-product blocks; the containing cycle length is uniform on \(1,\ldots,m_d\), and the total rotation sum is uniform modulo \(d\). The congruence \((k/\ell)S\equiv1\pmod d\) has probability \(1/d\) precisely when \(\ell\mid k\) and \(\gcd(d,k/\ell)=1\). Summation proves the formula; Möbius inversion and partition double-counting prove the rest. 230 direct fixed-power comparisons, 11 independently enumerated full profiles, and five partition-sum checks agree. Finite computations are corroboration, not proof.

originality.rationale: The strongest identified primary source (Kai arxiv:2609.17438) gives the action quandle and inner group, but not the exact power fixed-point formula, divisor/coprimality selection or complete profiles. Nelson provides generic profile-polynomial definitions, Lages et al. prove unrelated profile criteria, and Higashitani–Kurihara study a different quandle. Indexed literature and web searches returned no equivalent or stronger statement. Standard wreath centralizers, Möbius inversion, and the source iteration are acknowledged prior tools. Historical priority under alternate terminology remains possible.
residual_risks: An older matrix-rack or generalized-quandle-polynomial treatment might contain an equivalent fixed-power count under different terminology.
The comparisons check identifiable primary accessible sources; search results are not a proof of global uniqueness.

value.rationale: Exact right-translation profiles are standard algebraic quandle invariants relevant to classification and fixed-point polynomial statistics. The theorem determines every length and multiplicity uniformly in n and h from cycle multiplicities of h^k, a natural entire family arising from the Cayley-type universal embedding. The partition-sum expression for random fixed pairs is a second natural closed invariant. This is more than a renamed component count or tiny enumerative instance.
